C005.subject: GDP per capita
C005.object: material living standards for the bottom 40% of income earners in developed economies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita material living standards for the bottom 40% of income earners in developed economies]

[PATH:empirical] OECD Income Distribution Database (IDD) – decile shares and real income growth data for bottom 40% — Directly measures whether bottom 40% real income growth diverges from GDP per capita growth in OECD countries since the 1980s, providing a clear test of the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Piketty, Saez, and Zucman (2018) 'Distributional National Accounts' – DINA for developed economies — Provides comprehensive estimates of income growth across the full distribution, allowing comparison between GDP per capita and bottom 40% material living standards over time.

[PATH:theoretical] Meyer and Sullivan (2017) 'Consumption and Income Inequality in the U.S.' – consumption-based measures of material well-being — Offers a conceptual and empirical alternative to income-based measures; if consumption for the bottom 40% tracks GDP per capita more closely than income, it may refute the hypothesis that GDP per capita overestimates improvements.

C006.subject: GDP per capita
C006.predicate: is not a comprehensive measure of
C006.object: material living standards in developed economies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita material living standards in developed economies]

[PATH:empirical] OECD Better Life Index (BLI) composite indicators of well-being, including housing, income, jobs, community, education, environment, civic engagement, health, life satisfaction, safety, work-life balance — Directly compares GDP per capita with multidimensional material living standards across OECD countries to test whether GDP per capita alone captures or misses key material dimensions.

[PATH:literature] Stiglitz, Sen, Fitoussi (2009) 'Report by the Commission on the Measurement of Economic Performance and Social Progress' — Foundational theoretical and empirical critique arguing GDP is insufficient for measuring material well-being, providing both conceptual framework and evidence for the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Cross-national panel data on household disposable income, consumption expenditure, and wealth distribution (e.g., OECD Income Distribution Database, Luxembourg Income Study) — Tests whether GDP per capita trends align with trends in actual household material resources (income, consumption, wealth) in developed economies post-2000, revealing gaps.

C007.subject: GDP growth in highly unequal societies
C007.object: population-level subjective wellbeing and mental health
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP growth in highly unequal societies population-level subjective wellbeing and mental health]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal analysis of OECD panel data (e.g., World Happiness Report, Gallup World Poll) linking GDP growth, Gini coefficient, and self-reported life satisfaction or mental health indices (e.g., GHQ-12) from 2000-2020. — Directly tests the temporal correlation between GDP growth in unequal societies and subjective wellbeing, controlling for confounds like social safety nets.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies on income inequality and mental health outcomes (e.g., depression, anxiety) in OECD countries, focusing on within-country changes over time. — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether the inverse correlation holds consistently across different measures, populations, and time periods.

C008.subject: GDP growth
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP growth subjective wellbeing and mental health]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel studies (e.g., German Socio-Economic Panel, BHPS) linking GDP per capita growth to individual-level mental health indices (e.g., GHQ-12, SWLS) over 2000-2020 — Directly tests the temporal correlation between macroeconomic growth and subjective wellbeing at the individual level, controlling for confounders like unemployment or inequality.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of cross-country comparisons (e.g., World Happiness Report, OECD Better Life Index) examining the GDP-wellbeing relationship within OECD nations — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether the proxy relationship holds consistently across diverse cultural and policy contexts, addressing the 'Easterlin paradox'.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical work on relative income and adaptation (e.g., Kahneman & Deaton, 2010; Luhmann et al., 2012) critiquing GDP as a wellbeing proxy — Provides conceptual grounds for why GDP growth may fail to capture subjective wellbeing due to hedonic adaptation, social comparison, and non-material determinants, thus refuting the hypothesis.
